Governor: Louisiana elects its governor in odd-numbered years. The last election was 2023, and the next is scheduled for 2027. First, the official SBE statewide candidate list has no U.S. Senate section; its only Senate entries are for State Senator by district. Second, the official Kent County ballot PDF (elections.maryland.gov/elections/2026/general_ballots/Kent.pdf), which I fetched and read, has no U.S. Senate contest. So the races list only includes the governor race. Office name, candidate order, party labels and running mates match the Kent County ballot, where the contest is printed as 'Governor / Lt. Governor, Vote for 1', with each ticket shown as 'Name and Name'. The SBE list (updated 10/16/2026) shows all eight ticket members as Active. The Green and Working Class Party tickets were party-designated in June–July 2026. I found no Libertarian or unaffiliated governor candidate on the official list or the ballot. BallotReady also lists Cheryl Riley, Jamie Raskin and Nancy Wallace, but under other offices, not governor; Nancy Wallace appears on the SBE list in a non-governor section. Dates come from the SBE 2026 general election page. Measures were left out because they are outside the requested scope.

Colom', so check how his name is printed on the ballot. found_official_list is false because the SOS page is a qualifying list ('candidates currently on file'), not a certified general election ballot or sample ballot. Where the names come from: I opened the Minnesota Secretary of State's candidate filings database (candidates.sos.mn.gov) for U.S. Senator and for Governor & Lt Governor. For Senate, Fox 9 and Wikipedia report that Peggy Flanagan won the DFL primary over Angie Craig and others, and that Michele Tafoya is the Republican nominee. For governor, NBC News and the Washington Post report that Amy Klobuchar won the DFL primary with 89.7% and that Lisa Demuth beat Mike Lindell and Kendall Qualls. The other two Senate candidates filed under non-major-party labels and were not in a primary: Rebecca Whiting (Libertarian) and Marisa Simonetti (Independent). The other governor ticket is Steven Young and Jane Kirby (Green). BallotReady's general-election page lists the same Senate and governor fields. The filing database prints the Green candidate's name as 'Steven Young.' Some sources use 'Steve Young.' Name formats such as middle initials should also be checked against the certified ballot. Lieutenant governor is on a joint ticket with governor, so it is not listed as a separate race. Dates: the SOS flyer shows early voting Sept. 18 to Nov. 2 and advance registration by Oct. 13. The Nov. 2 absentee-request deadline comes from HeadCount, not from an SOS page. Fox 9 recommends applying by Oct. 20. The polling hours (7 a.m. to 8 p.m., with some small towns opening as late as 10 a.m.) are standard Minnesota law, but I did not confirm them on a page in this request. The official site is listed as sos.mn.gov. The SOS also sends voters to mnvotes.gov for sample ballots and polling places.

U.S. Senate: there is no U.S. Senate race in New York in 2026. The state's official amended certification (dated Oct. 7, 2026) lists only these offices: Governor and Lt. Governor, Comptroller, Attorney General, Representative in Congress, State Senator, Member of Assembly and Supreme Court Justice. Neither Schumer's nor Gillibrand's seat is up this year, so the races list has only the governor race. Governor: I pulled the certification PDF from elections.ny.gov and read it myself. The race has five party lines. Democratic and Working Families: Hochul and Adams. Republican, Conservative and Vote Affordable: Blakeman and Hood. New York uses fusion voting, so each candidate appears on more than one line. The party field joins the line names as printed, and I kept each candidate as one entry. No other candidates are certified. Some secondary sources say otherwise: the Ithacan lists Jean Anglade (Independent) and Jonathan Makeley (Prohibition); Ballotpedia lists Larry Sharpe (L) and Anglade; Election Desk says Sharpe and Shannon Joy Bones would run on a 'Coalition' line and that Working Families would keep placeholders Amy Taylor and Joshua Goldfein instead of backing Hochul. None of them appear in the Oct. 7 official certification. The Working Families line shows Hochul and Adams, which matches AMNY's Oct. 22 voter guide. I left those other names out. Names are written as certified (Kathy C. Hochul, Bruce A. Blakeman, Adrienne E. Adams, Todd Hood). Dates: I checked these against NYC Votes, Vote.NYC, WRVO and LWV. I couldn't fetch the state's HTML certification page (url_not_accessible), but the PDF version fetched without trouble. Today is Oct. 23, so the registration and mail-application deadlines (Oct. 24) are tomorrow.

proposed.summary: N'Kiyla "Jasmine" Thomas is a nurse from Ardmore and a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. This is her first political campaign. She led the five-way June 16, 2026 Democratic primary for Oklahoma's open U.S. Senate seat, then defeated Jim Priest in the August 25, 2026 runoff to win the Democratic nomination for the November 3 general election.

positions.stance: Supports a single-payer "Medicare for All" system and says she aims to achieve it during a six-year term. She cites her nursing experience and rural access to care.
Supports universal childcare and parental leave.
Opposes defunding the Department of Defense, a position on which she says she differs from the Democratic Socialists of America platform. Her husband serves in the U.S. military.
Her campaign says she is committed to preserving tribal sovereignty and to working with Native leaders to protect tribal land, rights and cultural heritage.
Supports strengthening the Clean Water Act, protecting tribal water sovereignty, holding polluters accountable and investing in rural water infrastructure.
Has pledged not to accept contributions from corporate PACs.
Describes herself as a democratic socialist. She argues that working-class Oklahomans have been failed by a political class more focused on donors than on constituents.

positions.stance: Supports vetting immigrants and enforcing current immigration laws. Says the border must not allow large numbers of illegal crossings and argues the humanitarian crisis should be handled on the Mexico side of the border.
Supports a 'peace through strength' foreign policy. Proposes stopping U.S. land sales to China, especially near military bases.
Supports U.S. withdrawal from the Paris climate accords and says the U.S. can switch its coal-fired power generation to natural gas.
Says current federal law is adequate and supports requiring photo ID to vote. Says people without birth certificates can use census records to get a government-approved ID.

Supports a focus on mental health and enforcing existing gun laws. Says red flag laws do not deter gun violence, opposes abolishing the Second Amendment, and supports no-parole prison sentences for gang members.
Supports stopping deficit spending, balancing the federal budget, and using any surplus to pay down the national debt.
Calls fentanyl poisoning the top killer of young adults and says Congress should address it as a priority.
Opposes what he calls 'woke' policies in schools. Calls for ending the FBI threat tag used for school board threats, which he says has targeted parents who speak at board meetings.

Opposes the SAVE Act. Says voter ID is already required and that requiring a Real ID to vote would amount to a poll tax.

positions.stance: Supports vetting immigrants and enforcing current immigration laws. He wants to stop large numbers of people from crossing the border illegally, and says the crisis should be handled humanely by acting on the Mexican side of the border.

Proposes that the U.S. switch all of its coal-fired electricity generation to natural gas. He supports leaving the Paris climate agreement and argues that countries such as China and India are expanding coal power.

Supports a 'peace through strength' approach. Proposes ending land sales to China, especially near military bases.
Calls fentanyl a leading cause of death among young adults. Proposes charging people who sell it with capital murder.
Says he opposes 'woke policies' in schools. Wants the FBI to drop the threat tag it used for school board threats, which he says has been applied to parents who speak at school board meetings.

proposed.occupation: Colorado state senator (Senate District 4); aerospace engineer
proposed.summary: Mark Baisley is a Republican state senator who has represented Colorado Senate District 4 since 2023, after serving in the Colorado House from 2019 to 2023. He received at least 30% of the vote at the Republican state assembly, the only candidate to do so, and was unopposed in the June 30, 2026 Republican primary. He faces Democratic incumbent John Hickenlooper and minor-party candidates in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Says his main goal in the Senate is to make living costs more affordable by reducing the footprint of government.
Proposes shrinking the federal government and eventually replacing federal income taxes with revenue from tariffs.
Cites his 2024 measure SCR24B-002, which he says would make local government funding reliable and end large swings in property taxes. He says the approach would work in other states too.
Proposes giving lenders incentives so first-time homebuyers can get mortgage rates pegged to the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield.
Supports building more tunnels and storage to carry Western Slope water to the Front Range. He says Front Range use leaves little water for farms on the eastern plains.
Defended President Trump's war in Iran during an October 2026 debate. He argued that high gas prices are a necessary cost of confronting terrorism.

His campaign site says America is enriched by immigrants and that lawful immigrants should be self-reliant and assimilate. Axios reports he supports deporting immigrants deemed dangerous while letting vetted legal immigrants stay.
Opposes abortion rights and said in a debate that he would vote for a national abortion ban.
Told the state GOP assembly that he intends to partner with the Trump administration in the Senate.
Opposed moving U.S. Space Command headquarters out of Colorado.

proposed.summary: Andrew Gerena, who goes by the military callsign "Jeranimo," is an independent candidate for U.S. Senate in Tennessee. He is from Knoxville and filed on March 9, 2026. He qualified for the November 3, 2026 general election ballot by petition.

positions.stance: Says the health care system is corrupt and profit-based and calls for fixing it. Supports letting veterans choose their own health care providers and modernizing the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Proposes moving federal money from the military budget to education, infrastructure, research and job training. Supports required financial literacy classes in all high schools.
Supports expanding protections for parks and wildlife and strict environmental and data privacy rules for AI data centers. Proposes building modern nuclear and renewable power plants.
Opposes any tax increase. Says too much tax money goes to regime-change wars and corporate tax breaks, and proposes moving military spending to domestic programs.

Proposes ending military aid to any country suspected of war crimes. Calls for separating U.S. military and intelligence agencies from all branches of the Israeli government, and for investigating AIPAC for espionage and treason.
Supports repealing the Patriot Act and ending all public-facing mass surveillance systems. Calls for investigating executives and engineers at companies that conduct mass surveillance.
Proposes making the death penalty available, by jury decision only, for people convicted of child sex offenses or trafficking. Wants to prioritize fighting human, drug and weapons trafficking.
Proposes making it a felony to use AI to produce news or informational content about real people, events or subjects.
Supports building high-speed passenger rail across the country and bringing back modern terminals where truckers can rest, transfer loads and make repairs.
Supports right-to-repair protections, saying they defend farmers and working-class people.

He won the May 19, 2026 Republican primary for governor against Ken McFeeters and Will Santivasci, and he is the Republican nominee on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot. He faces Democrat Doug Jones, a former U.S. Senator.

proposed.occupation: State senator (Oxford County) and businessman
proposed.summary: Richard A. "Rick" Bennett, 63, of Oxford, is a Maine state senator and served as Maine Senate President from 2001 to 2002. He served in the Legislature for many years as a Republican. He announced on June 24, 2025, that he would run for governor as an independent, and he is on the November 3, 2026 general election ballot against Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles.

positions.stance: Proposes lower down payments for first-time homebuyers and direct mortgage assistance. Also proposes reviving Maine's factory-built housing industry, expanding home repair programs, and removing permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks.
Supports expanding the Property Tax Fairness Credit and increasing state funding for county jails to reduce pressure on county taxes.

Proposes appointing Public Utilities Commissioners who would review and lower the guaranteed equity returns of Maine's investor-owned utilities to reduce delivery costs. Also proposes lowering energy costs for manufacturers and heritage industries.
Says he would not govern as a partisan and calls for collaboration and compromise. Proposes weekly Blaine House dinners with Republican and Democratic legislative leaders.
Says restoring public trust that tax dollars are spent wisely would be a first-year priority.
As a legislator, opposed MaineCare expansion and public funding for Planned Parenthood, according to Bangor Daily News reporting.

history: Maine House of Representatives, 1990–1994
Maine Senate, 1996–2004 and 2020–present (Oxford County)
President of the Maine Senate, 2001–2002

Education: BA, Harvard University; MBA, University of Southern Maine

proposed.occupation: Software developer
proposed.summary: Stephen Villee is a software developer who moved to New Hampshire in 2003 as one of the earliest Free State Project participants. He was the Libertarian nominee for governor in 2024 and received about 2% of the vote. In 2026 the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire's convention did not back his campaign, so an independent group of Libertarians gathered petition signatures that put him on the November ballot as the Libertarian candidate.

positions.stance: Says that in the long term he wants to reduce or eliminate both public school funding and Education Freedom Accounts, but that this must wait until more libertarians move to New Hampshire.
Says that in the long term he wants to reduce or eliminate public school funding.
Supports making cannabis fully legal for adults. Cites the House passing HB360 in 2023 before it failed in the Senate.
Proposes adopting approval voting in New Hampshire elections and says it solves the 'spoiler problem' faced by third-party candidates.
Supports 'Defend the Guard' legislation, which would bar activating the New Hampshire National Guard for combat unless Congress officially declares war.
Supports legalizing medical psilocybin for PTSD, substance use disorder and treatment-resistant depression.
States a long-term goal of winding down welfare programs, with grandfathering for people already living in New Hampshire.
Says that as a long-term goal he wants to negotiate a peaceful secession from the United States to free residents from the federal income tax.

Proposes a Tennessee Outcomes Commissioner under the Comptroller. The post would have a six-year term that spans changes of governor, and its job would be tracking public accountability.

proposed.occupation: Attorney; former Alaska Attorney General
proposed.summary: Treg Taylor is a Republican attorney who served as Alaska Attorney General from 2021 to 2025, and before that as deputy attorney general for the civil division. He resigned as attorney general in August 2025 and announced his campaign for governor in September 2025. He advanced from the August 18, 2026 top-four primary to the November 3 ranked-choice general election, with Candice (Candi) English as his running mate for lieutenant governor.

positions.stance: Supports a sustainable constitutional framework that provides meaningful, predictable dividends while protecting the Permanent Fund for future generations. Says the PFD should stop being used as a political weapon.

Argues that Alaska needs an economy strong enough that the state isn't constantly choosing between dividends and essential services, and says more production, jobs and investment would ease pressure on the budget.
Opposes levying new taxes to pay for larger dividends. Argues that the state should grow the economy to raise revenue rather than add to the tax burden on Alaskans.

Says the question is whether students are succeeding, not only how much the state spends. Supports accountability, transparency and flexibility, along with a funding system that puts students and teachers first.
Wants to improve reading proficiency and expand vocational education.

Supports regulatory and permitting reform, increased Cook Inlet natural gas production and the Alaska LNG project. Proposes opening more land for Alaskans to own and accelerating infrastructure to lower energy and housing costs.

Says his approach to federal fisheries is 'Alaskan fish for Alaska, Alaskans first.' Says no single user of a fishery should profit at the expense of other users, and notes that the governor appoints members of the North Pacific Fishery Management Council.
Proposes modernizing state government, eliminating duplication and improving technology so that state services are faster and more responsive.
Lists unlocking timber, minerals and rare earths as a priority, along with energy, land and permitting reform as ways to grow the economy.
His official election pamphlet statement pledges to protect girls' sports and stop what he calls 'woke indoctrination' in schools.

proposed.occupation: North Dakota Public Service Commissioner (incumbent, appointed January 2025); certified public accountant
proposed.summary: Jill Kringstad is a Republican who has served on the North Dakota Public Service Commission since Governor Kelly Armstrong appointed her in January 2025 to fill the seat Julie Fedorchak left after being elected to the U.S. House. Before her appointment she worked on the PSC staff starting in 2016. She won the June 2026 Republican primary for the unexpired two-year term against Chris Olson and faces Democratic-NPL candidate Scot Kelsh in the November 3, 2026 general election.

positions.stance: Says her accounting background lets her check whether costs in utility rate requests are reasonable. She cites the Xcel Energy case, where the PSC approved about a 10% increase after a request of more than 19%.

Opposes letting power providers pass data center costs on to residential and other existing customers. Says data centers should pay their own way, and wants their benefits to customers, such as bill credits, made easier to see.

Championed a state law that separates technical hearings from local public-testimony hearings. Says the PSC should not cheerlead for developers, and that projects from developers who don't treat landowners with respect should face a harder path.
Says baseload coal and natural gas are needed during extreme North Dakota winters, calling reliability in those conditions a safety issue. Says four-hour battery storage is not enough.
Says North Dakota has the nation's lowest residential electricity rates and pledges to keep them low while ensuring the state has abundant, reliable power.
